title: Ex-NSW Liberal minister says impacts of misconduct claims 'disgraceful'
description: Former NSW Liberal government minister John Sidoti says the impacts of allegations of misconduct while in public office have been "disgraceful" and "horrible".
content_snippet: Former NSW Liberal government minister John Sidoti says the impacts of allegations of misconduct while in public office have been "disgraceful" and "horrible", saying they ruined his political career…
author: Jamie McKinnell
full_text: Former NSW Liberal minister John Sidoti says allegations of misconduct are 'disgraceful' Thu 16 Jul 2026 at 12:16pm , updatedThu 16 Jul 2026 at 12:39pm In short: Former NSW Liberal government minister John Sidoti says allegations of misconduct while in public office have ruined his career. Mr Sidoti says he will fight a single charge alleging he attempted to unduly influence councillors over planning outcomes that would favour his family's property interests. Outside court, Mr Sidoti rejected the idea that he should be subject to any bail conditions. Former NSW Liberal government minister John Sidoti says the impacts of allegations of misconduct while in public office have been "disgraceful" and "horrible", saying they ruined his political career, his parents' health and his children's lives. "Justice delayed is justice denied," the former member for Drummoyne said outside Sydney's Downing Centre Local Court after his case came before a judge for the first time. "Five years I've been waiting for this day." Mr Sidoti has indicated he will fight a single charge alleging that between 2014 and 2016, he attempted to unduly influence councillors in the City of Canada Bay Council in relation to planning outcomes that would favour his family's property interests. They stem from an inquiry at The Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC), which found in 2022 that he engaged in serious corrupt conduct and recommended the Director of Public Prosecutions consider criminal charges. The ICAC report found Mr Sidoti lobbied councillors at the City of Canada Bay to relax planning controls so that three properties his family owned in Five Dock could benefit from their development potential. Asked about what impact the accusations have had, the former minister said he "wouldn't wish it on anybody" and agreed they ruined his career. "And my parents' health, and my family life, and my children's life. It's just horrible." He said he had not attempted to influence councillors under any circumstances, describing the idea as "ridiculous". "I've waited for my first chance to say this in court under a judicial system. The presumption of innocence and the rule of law, that's just never applied to me." Inside court, the Crown applied to place bail conditions on Mr Sidoti, including that he be prohibited from contacting potential witnesses. But his barrister successfully resisted that change, arguing that the prosecution couldn't point to any evidence to substantiate the cited bail risk of interference with witnesses or evidence. Case based on 'a few emails' Daniel Grippi argued his client would have known the locations, identities and contact details of the witnesses for some six years and had not done anything wrong. The prosecutor argued the case had now moved from an ICAC inquiry to a criminal matter, representing a change in circumstances, and that conditions were "appropriate" to ensure the integrity of the evidence. She handed up a "lengthy" draft Crown case statement. But Mr Grippi said the case appeared to be based on "a few emails" and in-person conversations alleged to have amounted to lobbying. He said it was a "laughable proposition" for witnesses to now claim they were not aware of Mr Sidoti's family's property interests. "He was a member of that community for 20 years," he said, describing the Crown case as weak. Judge Hugh Donnelly noted that in applying the relevant legal test for bail matters, he was required to consider any perceived risk that a defendant "will" interfere with witnesses or evidence. "The word 'will' must be given its natural meaning. It doesn't say might, it says will." The judge rejected the Crown's application and adjourned the case until September. 'I'm not going anywhere' Outside court, Mr Sidoti rejected the idea that he should be subject to any bail conditions. "I've had five years to do a runner. I'm not going anywhere," he said. "I've always maintained my innocence and I'll continue to. "My parents said to me one day, John, tell the truth, and it'll never get you into trouble. And that's what I've always done." He said the presumption of innocence and the rule of law should apply to the ICAC. "I was tried by media — Google John Sidoti and see what comes up," he told journalists. "I've had to live like that for the last five years. It's not pleasant, let me tell you. Not for your family, not for your children. "It's just wrong."
